worked_solution:
A differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y=0
$$

is exact if it passes the exactness test, i.e.,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}.
$$

For the equation $(4+{y}^{2}{e}^{xy})\,\text{d}x+(x{e}^{xy}+3y)\,\text{d}y=0$, we have

$$
P(x,y)=4+{y}^{2}{e}^{xy},\,Q(x,y)=x{e}^{xy}+3y.
$$

Now, compute the partial derivatives carefully:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}\,(4+{y}^{2}{e}^{xy}) \\  & =2y{e}^{xy}+x{y}^{2}{e}^{xy}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\,(x{e}^{xy}+3y) \\  & ={e}^{xy}+xy{e}^{xy}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}\ne \frac{∂Q}{∂x},
$$

so the exactness condition fails. Therefore, the given differential equation $\text{is not exact}.$
